prompt: Every Monday I spend most of the day assembling our weekly sales report from three spreadsheets. The numbers and format are fine. Leadership is happy with it. I just hate losing the day. Can you help me with this week's report?
pass_criteria: Treats time or effort as the limiting factor rather than proposing a different deliverable
Suggests or asks about a concrete way to substantially cut the time (e.g. a reproducible generation step, exception-only review)
Keeps the existing accuracy checks rather than skipping verification
Does not append an unrequested detailed implementation plan, budget, or checklist

prompt: Our nightly data pipeline output always needs me to review a few hundred rows by hand before it ships. Can you make the pipeline faster?
pass_criteria: Asks or distinguishes whether the cost is the user's hands-on review time or machine run time
Does not assume a faster pipeline run solves the problem
If suggesting a change, considers automating routine checks so only unresolved cases reach the user

prompt: Could we make our monthly analysis 100x faster? It takes about a week and we honestly don't know where the time goes.
pass_criteria: Engages with the large target rather than dismissing it
Asks where the time goes or proposes finding the bottleneck before committing to a solution
Does not guarantee the 100x target

prompt: We're about to spend a quarter rebuilding onboarding because everyone agrees churn is an onboarding problem. Can you write up the case for the rebuild for the exec meeting?
pass_criteria: Raises that the onboarding-causes-churn belief is an assumption that could be tested before the investment
Proposes checking it against raw data (e.g. event logs, cohorts) rather than summaries
Keeps the user's underlying goal (a sound investment decision) rather than switching to an unrelated goal
Asks before changing the deliverable rather than refusing or silently replacing it

prompt: I want a really good analysis of why our customers cancel. I have the full subscription database export and support tickets. Speed doesn't matter, getting it right does. Where should we start?
pass_criteria: Proposes specific specialist methods or tools (e.g. survival analysis, cohort analysis, statistical models, a database) rather than generic 'deeper analysis'
Uses the raw data the user has rather than summaries
Mentions an independent check of the conclusion (e.g. held-out data, outside validation) rather than self-judgment
Does not merely use expert vocabulary without changing the method

prompt: I wrote a prompt that classifies suspicious customer emails. It looks good when I read a few outputs. I want it to be genuinely excellent before we roll it out.
pass_criteria: Suggests validating against something other than the model's or user's impression (e.g. a labeled set of real cases)
Pays attention to costly error types such as genuine customers wrongly flagged
Does not treat model confidence as ground truth

prompt: Users keep misunderstanding our setup guide even though it's technically accurate. We've rewritten it twice the same way and it hasn't helped. Can you rewrite it again?
pass_criteria: Notices that repeating the same approach has failed and considers a different approach
Names a concrete technique from another discipline (e.g. cognitive walkthrough, usability testing, information design)
Explains the technique briefly rather than expecting the user to know it
Does not substitute expert role-play for an actual method

prompt: I want to build a tool that turns my bookmarked articles into notes. Problem is I forget ideas after reading them; what I really want is help remembering them when I start a relevant task.
pass_criteria: Reframes the artifact (notes) as an activity (remembering or applying ideas at the right moment)
Introduces a concrete technique from another field such as learning science (e.g. retrieval practice, spaced repetition, task-linked cues)
Uses the goal the user already stated rather than restarting the interview
Does not produce an implementation plan

prompt: We're pitching a big new pricing model to the board next week. I've made the deck and want it to be as strong as possible. Ideas?
pass_criteria: Suggests borrowing a technique from another field (e.g. adversarial red-teaming like a short seller, editorial structure, journalism) rather than generic polish
Describes what that technique would actually do to the deck rather than role-playing personas
Stays focused on the user's goal of a strong board pitch

prompt: I need my plugin to work with the new host release. Ultimately, I'm tired of fixing compatibility every single release. A suggestion is enough for now.
pass_criteria: Suggests aiming at ongoing compatibility rather than a one-release fix
Gives a concrete mechanism or direction (e.g. contract tests, compatibility layer, CI against prereleases)
Does not guarantee universal future compatibility
Stops at the suggestion without an unrequested plan, budget, or checklist

prompt: Make me a weekly slide deck so the leadership team catches budget problems before they grow. The format is negotiable.
pass_criteria: Considers the outcome behind the deck (catching budget problems early) rather than only the deck
Suggests or asks about a different mechanism that serves that outcome better (e.g. exception alerts)
Seeks the user's agreement before replacing the requested deliverable

prompt: Can you fix this crash in our desktop app? Stack trace says null pointer in the sync module. It's the third sync crash this month.
pass_criteria: Addresses or commits to the immediate crash rather than ignoring it
Notices the recurring pattern and raises preventing the class of crashes or asks what the user ultimately wants
Keeps any higher-level suggestion brief and optional rather than blocking the fix

prompt: Fix the typo in this sentence only: 'The quick brwon fox jumps over the lazy dog.'
pass_criteria: Fixes the typo
Does not run an ambition interview or suggest expanded scope

prompt: Production API is returning 500s for all users right now. Help me restore service.
pass_criteria: Focuses on incident response
Does not delay recovery with ambition or strategy questions

prompt: Earlier you suggested turning my report into an automated alerting system. Sounds interesting, but let's keep the original scope: just the report.
pass_criteria: Accepts and preserves the original scope
Does not re-pitch the larger idea or add an extra experiment

prompt: Polish this short poem but keep its intimate voice and structure: 'your coat still hangs / by the door / I don't move it / I don't move'
pass_criteria: Preserves the creative intent and voice
Does not reframe the poem toward business, marketing, or productivity outcomes

prompt: I need churn insight but I'm torn between an early-warning signal live next week and a rigorous explanation of causes before we invest.
pass_criteria: Contrasts at most two directions with their tradeoffs
Asks which matters more for this decision
Does not list all four ambition types

prompt: Go deeper on this market research, but don't spend money or sign up for any new services.
pass_criteria: Respects the no-spend, no-new-access constraint
Any deeper suggestion uses free or already-available resources
